# How to use this subject

General Pharmacy is the first "medicines" subject of the new B.Pharm (NEP 2020) course. It is a 3-credit theory course: 45 lecture hours, 75 marks in all (30 sessional, 45 end-semester). It joins three kinds of learning: descriptive theory (history, scope, pharmacopoeias, prescription), **numericals** (alligation, proof spirit, isotonicity, dilution, posology, displacement value) and **dosage forms** (powders, tablets, capsules, liquids, semisolids, suppositories). Study one unit a day: read the notes, redo every worked example with a calculator without looking, write the tables and diagrams from memory, then answer the questions for that unit.

The notes follow the five units of the PCI B.Pharm Syllabus 2026 exactly; no unit is split or joined. All drugs and numbers in the worked calculations are made up for practice, and the posology section gives the formulas as fractions of the adult dose rather than doses of real drugs.

**End-semester paper (PCI Table XV, 3-credit course): 45 marks, 2 hours.** Confirm the exact pattern with your university.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Multiple-choice / objective questions, all compulsory | 10 × 1 = 10 |
| II | Short answers: answer 5 of 7 | 5 × 4 = 20 |
| III | Long answers: answer 2 of 3 | 2 × 7.5 = 15 |

In this app the long answers are marked out of 8 (the app uses whole marks), so the full mock paper totals 46. The model long answers are written for 7.5 marks: about one and a half pages, with a definition, a table or diagram, and 6–8 well-made points. Short answers (4 marks) need about half a page: definition, 3–5 points or a small table, one example.

**Probability ratings**

- **High**: a standard topic of this syllabus that is asked in most papers on the same content; prepare the full answer.
- **Medium**: asked every few years, or as part of a larger question.
- **Low**: less common; useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from the weight of each topic in the syllabus and from how often similar questions appear in pharmaceutics papers. This is a new syllabus, so there are no past papers of this exact course yet; treat the ratings as guidance, not a promise.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics to prepare first |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Profession of pharmacy | Parts of a prescription and its handling; Latin terms; IP structure and a model monograph; scope of pharmacy in community, hospital, clinical and industrial practice; milestones (Chopra Committee, Pharmacy Act, PCI, first IP) |
| 2 Calculations and dosage forms | Alligation, proof spirit, isotonicity (FPD and NaCl equivalent), dilution numericals; geometric dilution; posology rules; classification of dosage forms and routes; definition and ideal properties of excipients |
| 3 Solid dosage forms | Classification of powders; effervescent, efflorescent, hygroscopic powders and eutectic mixtures; types of tablets; wet granulation; types and sizes of capsules |
| 4 Liquids | Syrups, elixirs, aromatic waters, linctus; definitions with examples of external liquids; flocculated vs deflocculated suspensions; emulsifying agents and identification tests; dry gum method |
| 5 Semisolids and suppositories | Classification of ointment bases; methods of preparing ointments and creams; ideal suppository base; types of bases; displacement value numerical |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Open every answer with a one-line definition and an example. Examiners give marks for both.
2. Numericals: write the formula, substitute with units, and box the answer with its unit (g, ml, % w/v, degrees proof, g NaCl per 100 ml). Method marks are given even if the arithmetic slips.
3. Learn these numbers cold: proof spirit 57.1% v/v and factor 1.753; FP of blood −0.52 °C; FPD of 1% NaCl 0.576 °C; 0.9% NaCl isotonic; adult BSA 1.73 m²; Simple Syrup IP 66.7% w/w; effervescent ratio 1 : 2 : 3.44; dry gum 4:2:1, 3:2:1, 2:2:1; capsule sizes 000 to 5.
4. Use comparison tables (flocculated vs deflocculated, O/W vs W/O, liniment vs lotion, hard vs soft capsules, the four classes of ointment base). A neat table can earn full marks in a 4-mark answer.
5. Draw small labelled diagrams: prescription layout, alligation cross, settled suspensions, percolator, wet-granulation flow chart, suppository fusion steps.
6. For a long answer on any dosage form, follow one order: definition → types → advantages and disadvantages → excipients → method of preparation → examples → storage and labelling.
7. Do all ten MCQs: they are compulsory and quick; the MCQ bank here covers the facts they usually test.

# Last-night revision sheet

## Unit 1: Profession of pharmacy

- Chopra Committee (1930–31) → Drugs Act 1940 (now Drugs and Cosmetics Act) and Rules 1945; Pharmacy Act 1948 → PCI 1949; first IP 1955.
- Prof. M. L. Schroff (BHU): father of pharmacy education in India. P. C. Ray: Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works (first Indian firm).
- Scope: community (dispensing, counselling), hospital (procurement, formulary, P&T committee), clinical (ward rounds, ADR monitoring), industry (R&D, production, QC, QA, regulatory).
- IP: IP Commission, Ghaziabad; BP 1864; USP 1820 (USP–NF); BPC 1907; Ph. Int. by WHO; NFI = guide to rational use.
- IP layout: general notices → general chapters (appendices) → monographs. Monograph: title, formula, definition, category, description, solubility, identification, tests, assay, storage, labelling.
- Prescription: superscription (Rx) · inscription (drugs) · subscription (to pharmacist) · signatura (to patient). Doubts → prescriber. Write 0.5 mg, never .5 mg.
- Latin: a.c. before food, p.c. after food, b.d. twice, t.d.s. thrice, q.i.d. four times, h.s. bedtime, stat. at once, s.o.s. if needed, q.s. enough, M. mix, gtt. drops.

## Unit 2: Calculations and dosage forms

| Topic | Key formula or fact |
| --- | --- |
| Dilution | C1V1 = C2V2 |
| Alligation alternate | Parts of higher = wanted − lower; parts of lower = higher − wanted; diluent = 0% |
| Proof spirit | 57.1% v/v = 100° proof; degree proof = % v/v × 1.753; > 100 OP, < 100 UP |
| Isotonic (FPD) | W = (0.52 − a)/b; b(NaCl) = 0.576; 0.9% NaCl isotonic |
| NaCl equivalent | NaCl to add = 0.009 × V − (g drug × E) |
| White–Vincent | V (ml water) = W × E × 111.1 |
| Young's | Age/(Age + 12) × adult dose |
| Clark's | Weight (lb)/150 × adult dose |
| Fried's | Age (months)/150 × adult dose |
| Dilling's | Age/20 × adult dose |
| BSA | Child BSA/1.73 × adult dose |

- Geometric dilution: add diluent equal to the mass already in the mortar.
- Dosage forms: solid, liquid (monophasic, biphasic), semisolid, gaseous.
- Excipient: inert, non-toxic, compatible, stable, cheap, official grade; diluent, binder, disintegrant, lubricant, preservative, etc.

## Unit 3: Solids

- Powders: bulk (internal, external) and divided. Surgical dusting powder sterile.
- Effervescent: citric : tartaric : NaHCO3 = 1 : 2 : 3.44; fusion or wet (alcohol) method; airtight.
- Efflorescent (alum, citric acid) → anhydrous form. Hygroscopic/deliquescent → waxed paper, airtight. Eutectic (camphor + menthol) → adsorbent (light MgO, kaolin).
- Tablets: compressed (plain, layered, sugar/film/enteric coated, chewable, effervescent, buccal, sublingual, lozenge) or moulded (tablet triturates); pills = rolled spheres.
- Wet granulation: mix → wet mass → screen → dry → size → lubricate → compress. Dry granulation: slugging/roller compaction.
- Capsules: hard two-piece, soft one-piece (plasticiser glycerin/sorbitol); sizes 000 (1.37 ml) … 0 (0.68 ml) … 5 (0.13 ml); punch method by hand.

## Unit 4: Liquids

- Aromatic water: distillation, solution with talc, concentrate 1 + 39.
- Simple Syrup IP 66.7% w/w; problems: crystallisation, fermentation, inversion.
- Elixir: sweet hydroalcoholic; add aqueous to alcoholic slowly. Linctus: viscous, sip undiluted, cough.
- Liniment rubbed; lotion dabbed; throat paint glycerin base; gargle and mouthwash not swallowed; enema evacuant or retention; eye drops sterile isotonic; no oily nasal drops; tincture by maceration or percolation.
- Suspension: flocculated (fast settling, loose, no cake) vs deflocculated (slow, cake). Stokes: v = 2r²(ρs − ρl)g/9η. Methods: dispersion, precipitation. F = Vu/Vo.
- Emulsion: O/W, W/O, multiple. Tests: dilution, dye, conductivity, fluorescence, CoCl2 paper. Dry gum 4:2:1 fixed, 3:2:1 mineral, 2:2:1 volatile; wet gum; bottle method. HLB 3–6 W/O, 8–18 O/W.

## Unit 5: Semisolids and suppositories

- Ointment bases: oleaginous (soft paraffin), absorption (wool fat; hydrous wool fat), water-removable (emulsifying ointment), water-soluble (PEG).
- Methods: trituration, fusion (decreasing melting point, stir till cold), chemical reaction (non-staining iodine ointment), emulsification (creams, phases at about 70–75 °C).
- Paste: high powder content; gel: polymer network (carbomer + triethanolamine).
- Suppository (rectal), pessary (vaginal), bougie (urethral).
- Theobroma oil melts about 30–35 °C, polymorphic; glycero-gelatin hygroscopic, lubricate mould with liquid paraffin; PEG dissolves.
- Base needed = N × E − drug/DV; DV = drug ÷ base displaced; glycero-gelatin ≈ 1.2 × theobroma oil weight.

## Exam pattern (45 marks, 2 hours)

10 MCQs × 1 · 5 of 7 short × 4 · 2 of 3 long × 7.5. Box numerical answers with units.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a written or electronic order from a registered medical practitioner (or dentist or veterinarian) to a pharmacist to prepare and/or dispense a medicine for a named patient, with directions for use; it is a legal document.
2. Model layout (draw a box): prescriber's name, qualification, registration number and address; date; patient's name, age, sex, weight and address; Rx; drug names and quantities; directions to pharmacist; Sig. directions to patient; refill instruction; prescriber's signature.
3. Parts: superscription = Rx (Latin recipe, take thou); inscription = names and quantities of ingredients (main part); subscription = directions to the pharmacist on the dosage form and quantity to supply; signatura = directions to the patient, copied on the label; renewal instructions; signature and registration number make it legal.
4. Handling – receive: personally and politely.
5. Read and check: legality, completeness, legibility, dose, frequency, interactions and incompatibilities; clear doubts with the prescriber, never with the patient.
6. Collect and compound: check each label three times, weigh and measure accurately, one prescription at a time.
7. Pack and label: suitable container; label with patient name, drug, strength, directions, date, pharmacy name and auxiliary labels.
8. Record and deliver: enter in the prescription register; hand over with counselling on dose, timing, storage and side effects.
questions.question: Define prescription. Draw a model prescription and explain its parts. Describe how a pharmacist should handle a prescription.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: an official book, published under government authority, giving standards of identity, purity and strength of drugs and preparations with test methods; a monograph is the entry for one substance.
2. IP: first edition 1955 (after the Chopra Committee); later editions 1966, 1985, 1996, 2007, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022; published by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad; legal standard under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.
3. BP: first published 1864; prepared by the British Pharmacopoeia Commission and revised every year; official in the UK; includes European Pharmacopoeia texts.
4. USP: first published 1820 by the US Pharmacopeial Convention; issued as USP–NF (NF covers excipients); official in the USA.
5. International Pharmacopoeia: published by WHO; model standards, especially for essential medicines, which countries may adopt.
6. Others: BPC (1907, formulae and information), European, Japanese and Chinese pharmacopoeias; NFI is a formulary for rational use.
7. Structure of IP: front matter (preface, introduction, list of additions and omissions) → General Notices (rules for interpreting the book: percentages, temperatures, storage and solubility terms) → General Chapters/appendices (test methods, reagents, volumetric solutions) → general monographs on dosage forms → individual monographs (drug substances, excipients, dosage forms, vaccines, blood products, herbal, veterinary).
8. Monograph order: title, formula, definition and content limit, category, description, solubility, identification, tests, assay, storage, labelling.
questions.question: What is a pharmacopoeia? Give an account of the IP, BP, USP and International Pharmacopoeia. Describe the structure of the Indian Pharmacopoeia.

questions.answer:
1. Early period: Ayurveda (Charaka, Sushruta Samhitas), Unani and Siddha; the healer prepared medicines; British period compounders trained on the job; no law on drug quality.
2. Education: Prof. M. L. Schroff began university pharmacy teaching at BHU (degree course 1937), father of pharmacy education; Pharmacy Act 1948; PCI 1949 sets education standards; growth of D.Pharm, B.Pharm, M.Pharm; Pharm.D 2008; credit-based syllabus 2014; NEP 2020 syllabus 2026.
3. Industry: Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works by P. C. Ray (1901); Chopra Committee 1930–31 → Drugs Act 1940; public sector units (HAL, IDPL); Patents Act 1970 allowed process patents → generic boom, 'pharmacy of the world'; product patents from 2005 push research.
4. Organisations: PCI and State Pharmacy Councils, CDSCO under DCGI, IP Commission, IPA, APTI, Indian Pharmaceutical Congress Association, IDMA.
5. Scope – community: dispensing, counselling, OTC advice, health screening.
6. Hospital: procurement, storage, distribution, P&T committee and formulary, drug information.
7. Clinical: ward rounds, prescription review, ADR monitoring, discharge counselling.
8. Industry including R&D: formulation development, production, QC, QA, regulatory affairs, marketing; also government (Drug Inspector), teaching, clinical research.

2. Superscription: the symbol Rx (recipe, take thou).

4. Subscription: directions to the pharmacist: dosage form and quantity to supply.

6. Renewal instructions and the prescriber's signature, address and registration number make it complete and legal.

1. Community: dispense prescriptions as a registered pharmacist; check prescriptions for errors and interactions.
2. Counsel patients on dose, timing, storage and side effects; supply OTC medicines responsibly and refer when needed.
3. Keep legal records; maintain storage and cold chain; health promotion and screening.
4. Hospital: procurement, storage, inventory control and distribution to wards and outpatients.

questions.answer:
1. Title (official name) with chemical formula and molecular weight.
2. Definition: chemical name and permitted content range (per cent, often on dried basis).
3. Category and dose; description (appearance, odour); solubility in pharmacopoeial terms.
4. Identification: tests proving identity (IR spectrum, melting point, colour reactions).
5. Tests: purity limits – related substances, heavy metals, sulphated ash, loss on drying.
6. Assay: quantitative method; storage conditions; labelling requirements. Example: paracetamol monograph follows this order.

questions.answer:
1. NFI: a book of information on medicines for prescribers and pharmacists, first edition 1960, now published by the IP Commission.
2. Gives drugs in therapeutic groups with indications, contraindications, cautions, side effects, interactions and preparations.
3. Aim: rational use of medicines.
4. IP gives legal standards of identity, purity and strength with test methods; NFI is a guide to use, not a legal quality standard.

questions.answer:
1. Isotonic: a solution with the same osmotic pressure as a body fluid (blood, tears); it freezes at −0.52 °C. Hypotonic → cells swell (haemolysis); hypertonic → cells shrink (crenation).
2. Need: injections (especially large volume, intrathecal), eye drops, nasal drops and wound washes – to avoid pain, irritation and tissue damage. 0.9% w/v NaCl and 5% w/v dextrose are isotonic.
3. FPD method: W = (0.52 − a)/b, where W = g of adjusting substance per 100 ml, a = FPD of the unadjusted drug solution, b = FPD of 1% adjusting substance (NaCl 0.576 °C). Check: W = 0.52/0.576 = 0.90 g for plain NaCl.
4. Example: a 1% solution of drug X has FPD 0.10 °C → W = (0.52 − 0.10)/0.576 = 0.73 g NaCl per 100 ml.
5. NaCl equivalent (E): grams of NaCl osmotically equal to 1 g of drug.
6. Example: 60 ml of 2% drug Y (E 0.20): drug = 1.2 g → equivalent 0.24 g NaCl; NaCl needed for 60 ml = 0.54 g; add 0.54 − 0.24 = 0.30 g NaCl.
7. Other methods: White–Vincent (V = W × E × 111.1 ml of water), molar concentration method.
8. Note: use the unit of answer (g NaCl per stated volume) and check that W is positive; a negative W means the drug solution is already hypertonic.
questions.question: Define isotonic solution. Why must some preparations be isotonic? Describe the freezing point depression and sodium chloride equivalent methods of adjusting tonicity with one example of each.

questions.answer:
1. Posology: the branch of pharmacy dealing with doses (Greek posos = how much); dose = amount of drug given at one time to produce the desired effect.
2. Factors: age, body weight, body surface area, sex (pregnancy, lactation), route and time of administration, disease of liver or kidney, tolerance, idiosyncrasy and allergy, cumulation, drug interactions (synergism, antagonism), emotional and environmental factors, genetic factors.
3. Young's rule: child dose = Age (years)/(Age + 12) × adult dose (1–12 years). Example fraction: 6 years → 6/18 = 1/3 of adult dose.
4. Dilling's rule: Age/20 × adult dose; Cowling's rule: age at next birthday/24 × adult dose.
5. Fried's rule (infants): Age (months)/150 × adult dose; 18 months → 0.12 of the adult dose.
6. Clark's rule (weight): Weight (lb)/150 × adult dose; 44 lb → 0.29 of the adult dose. Per-kg dosing: dose per kg × weight.
7. BSA method (most accurate): child dose = BSA (m²)/1.73 × adult dose; BSA from nomogram or Mosteller √[height (cm) × weight (kg)/3600]; e.g. 120 cm and 25 kg → 0.91 m² → 0.53 of adult dose.
8. These are approximations; official references and the prescriber's order decide the actual dose.
questions.question: Define posology. Discuss the factors affecting dose. Give the formulas used to calculate a child's dose based on age, body weight and body surface area.

questions.answer:
1. Alligation: arithmetic method for mixing two strengths to get an intermediate strength. Alligation medial finds the strength of a mixture; alligation alternate finds the proportion to mix. A diluent counts as 0%.
2. Alligation alternate cross: higher strength gets (wanted − lower) parts; lower gets (higher − wanted) parts.
3. (a) 10% → 5 − 2 = 3 parts; 2% → 10 − 5 = 5 parts; total 8. 10% ointment = 400 × 3/8 = 150 g; 2% ointment = 400 × 5/8 = 250 g. Check: (150 × 10 + 250 × 2)/400 = 5%.
4. Proof spirit: ethanol–water mixture with 57.1% v/v ethanol at 51 °F (about 10.6 °C) = 100° proof; stronger = over proof (OP), weaker = under proof (UP).
5. Formulae: degree proof = % v/v × 1.753; OP = proof − 100; UP = 100 − proof; volume of proof spirit = volume × proof/100.
6. (b) 90% v/v × 1.753 = 157.8° proof = 57.8 OP; 40% v/v × 1.753 = 70.1° proof = 29.9 UP.
7. Use: excise duty and labelling of alcohol in medicines.
8. When diluting alcohol, make up to final volume because alcohol and water contract on mixing.

1. Method for mixing a small amount of a potent drug uniformly with a large amount of diluent.
2. Triturate the drug with an equal amount of diluent.
3. Add diluent equal to the amount already in the mortar and triturate; repeat, doubling each time, until all diluent is added.
4. Example: 50 mg drug + 50 mg lactose → 100 mg; + 100 mg → 200 mg; continue to 5 g, giving a 1% w/w trituration. A trace of inert colour can show uniform mixing.

1. Solid: powders, granules, tablets, capsules, pills, lozenges, suppositories.
2. Liquid – monophasic: solutions, syrups, elixirs, linctuses, aromatic waters, drops; biphasic: suspensions, emulsions.
3. Semisolid: ointments, creams, pastes, gels, jellies. Gaseous: aerosols, inhalations, sprays.
4. Routes: oral, sublingual/buccal, parenteral (IV, IM, SC, intradermal), rectal, vaginal, topical, transdermal, inhalation, ophthalmic, otic, nasal.

questions.answer:
1. Excipient: a substance other than the API intentionally added to a dosage form to help manufacture, protect, aid administration or control release; inactive at the amount used.
2. Ideal: inert, non-toxic, non-irritant, compatible with API, stable, does not harm bioavailability, acceptable taste and colour, cheap, available, of pharmacopoeial quality.
3. Importance: allow processing (flow, compression), protect drug (antioxidants, preservatives), mask taste, aid identification, control release, ensure uniform dose.
4. Examples: diluent lactose, binder starch paste, disintegrant sodium starch glycolate, lubricant magnesium stearate, preservative parabens.

1. Active pharmaceutical ingredient (drug substance): the component of a dosage form that produces the pharmacological or therapeutic effect.
2. Ideal: pure, of known identity and strength.
3. Stable to light, heat, moisture and air; suitable particle size, solubility and permeability for absorption.
4. Compatible with excipients; reproducible manufacture; safe and effective at the intended dose.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: mixtures of finely divided dry drugs/chemicals for internal or external use.
2. Classification: bulk powders – internal (antacids, laxatives, ORS) and external (dusting powders, insufflations, dentifrices, douche powders, snuffs); divided powders (chartulae) – simple or compound, packed in papers or sachets.
3. Advantages: more stable than liquids; fast dissolution; flexible dose; easy for those who cannot swallow tablets; large doses possible; cheap.
4. Disadvantages: taste not masked; bulk doses inaccurate; unsuitable for corrosive, deliquescent or volatile drugs; slow to divide.
5. Effervescent powders: acid (citric + tartaric) with sodium bicarbonate; in water release CO2, masking taste and aiding dissolution; ratio 1 : 2 : 3.44.
6. Preparation: fusion method (water of crystallisation of citric acid monohydrate acts as binder on warming; sieve and dry) or wet method (ethanol as moistening agent); store airtight.
7. Eutectic mixtures: solids that liquefy when mixed because the mixture melts below room temperature (camphor + menthol, camphor + phenol, menthol + thymol).
8. Handling: mix each separately with an adsorbent (light magnesium oxide, kaolin, starch) and combine lightly, or let liquefy and absorb; pack in waxed paper or capsules; store cool.
questions.question: Classify powders. Give their advantages and disadvantages. Write notes on effervescent powders and eutectic mixtures.

questions.answer:
1. Tablets: solid unit dosage forms of one or more drugs with or without excipients, made by compression or moulding.
2. Oral swallowed: plain compressed; multiple compressed (layered, compression-coated); sugar-coated; film-coated; enteric-coated (dissolve in intestine); chewable (antacids); sustained/controlled release.
3. Dissolved or dispersed first: effervescent, dispersible, soluble tablets.
4. Oral cavity: buccal and sublingual (absorbed directly, avoid first pass), lozenges/troches (local action in mouth and throat).
5. Other: vaginal tablets, implants; moulded tablets (tablet triturates: drug + lactose moistened and pressed into moulds, then dried); pills are rolled spherical masses (now rare).
6. Wet granulation: weigh and sift → dry mix drug, diluent, disintegrant → add binder solution to form a wet mass → pass through a sieve → dry granules → dry screening (sizing) → add lubricant, glidant and extragranular disintegrant → compress.
7. Why granulate: better flow, density and compressibility; prevents segregation; uniform dose.
8. Excipients named: lactose, starch paste/PVP, starch or sodium starch glycolate, magnesium stearate, talc/colloidal silica.
questions.question: Define tablets. Describe the various types of tablets with examples. Write the steps of the wet granulation method.

questions.answer:
1. Capsules: solid dosage forms in which drug and excipients are enclosed in a soluble shell, usually gelatin (type A from acid-treated pig skin, type B from alkali-treated bones and hides).
2. Hard capsules: two pieces (body and cap); shell of gelatin, water, colour, titanium dioxide; filled with powders, granules or pellets.
3. Soft capsules: one piece, sealed; thicker shell with plasticiser (glycerin or sorbitol); filled with oils, solutions or suspensions; made and filled in one step.
4. Others: HPMC (vegetarian) capsules; enteric and modified-release capsules.
5. Sizes: 000 (largest, about 1.37 ml), 00 (0.95), 0 (0.68), 1 (0.50), 2 (0.37), 3 (0.30), 4 (0.21), 5 (smallest, 0.13 ml); choose the smallest that holds dose plus diluent.
6. Hand (punch) method: spread powder on a slab to one-third body length; press the body into it repeatedly until full; fit the cap; weigh each capsule.
7. Capsule-filling boards fill many at once; automatic machines separate, fill (auger, dosator, tamping), rejoin and eject.
8. Advantages: tasteless, easy to swallow, fewer excipients; limitations: not for efflorescent or deliquescent drugs, animal origin, humidity-sensitive.
questions.question: Define capsules. Differentiate hard and soft gelatin capsules. Give capsule sizes and describe the methods of filling hard capsules.

questions.answer:
1. Efflorescent: crystalline substances that lose water of crystallisation in air, making a powder damp (alum, citric acid monohydrate, sodium carbonate decahydrate).
2. Handling: use an equivalent amount of the anhydrous form; pack in well-closed containers.
3. Hygroscopic: absorb moisture from air (ammonium chloride, potassium citrate); deliquescent absorb so much they dissolve (calcium chloride, zinc chloride).
4. Handling: work fast in a dry place, avoid very fine trituration, add adsorbent, wrap in waxed or double paper, pack airtight with desiccant.
questions.question: Write a note on efflorescent and hygroscopic powders.

questions.answer:
1. Fine powders applied to skin for lubricant, absorbent, protective, antiseptic or antipruritic action.
2. Medicated (intact skin) and surgical (wounds, body cavities – must be sterile).
3. Requirements: very fine, free from grit, free-flowing, uniform, non-irritant; talc and kaolin sterilised by dry heat because they may carry spores.
4. Bases: talc, starch, zinc oxide, kaolin; packed in sifter-top containers, labelled 'For external use only'. Example: zinc, starch and talc dusting powder.
questions.question: What are dusting powders? Give their requirements and an example.

questions.answer:
1. Advantages: accurate, uniform dose; most stable dosage form; easy to carry and take; cheap to make.
2. Taste masking and identification by coating, colour, shape, embossing; controlled or enteric release possible.
3. Disadvantages: difficult for children, elderly, unconscious patients to swallow; some drugs hard to compress.
4. Bitter drugs need coating; bioavailability problems for poorly soluble drugs; coating adds cost.
questions.question: Give the advantages and disadvantages of tablets.

questions.answer:
1. Moulded tablets (tablet triturates): drug with lactose (and sucrose) moistened with alcohol–water, pressed into a mould, pushed out and dried; small, flat, soft and quickly soluble; suit small doses of potent drugs.
2. Pills: small spherical masses made by rolling a plastic pill mass of drug and excipients (liquid glucose, syrup, acacia, liquorice) on a pill machine; may be coated.
3. Tablet triturates are made with moulds; pills by rolling and cutting.
4. Pills are now rarely made; both largely replaced by compressed tablets.
questions.question: Differentiate moulded tablets and pills.

questions.answer:
1. Diluent – lactose, microcrystalline cellulose; binder – starch paste, PVP.
2. Disintegrant – starch, sodium starch glycolate, croscarmellose sodium.
3. Lubricant – magnesium stearate; glidant – colloidal silica; anti-adherent – talc.
4. Colours, flavours and sweeteners for appearance and taste; wetting agent – sodium lauryl sulphate.
questions.question: List the excipients used in tablets with one example of each.

questions.answer: Citric acid : tartaric acid : sodium bicarbonate = 1 : 2 : 3.44 by weight.

questions.answer: Size 000 is the largest and size 5 the smallest.

questions.answer:
1. Suspension: biphasic liquid in which finely divided insoluble solid particles are dispersed uniformly in a liquid vehicle with the help of suspending agents.
2. Flocculated: particles form loose flocs; settle fast; clear supernatant; loose, bulky sediment; easily redispersed; no cake; less elegant.
3. Deflocculated: separate particles; settle slowly; cloudy supernatant; compact sediment that may cake; hard to redisperse; more elegant.
4. Stokes' law: v = 2r²(ρs − ρl)g/9η; settling slowed by small particles, high viscosity, small density difference.
5. Excipients: wetting agents (polysorbate 80, glycerin, alcohol); suspending agents – natural (acacia, tragacanth, alginate, xanthan), semisynthetic (methylcellulose, sodium CMC), clays (bentonite), synthetic (carbomer); flocculating agents (electrolytes, surfactants, polymers); buffers, preservatives, flavours, colours, sweeteners.
6. Dispersion method: wet the powder with a little wetting agent to a smooth paste; add the suspending agent dispersed in vehicle gradually; make up to volume (e.g. calamine lotion).
7. Precipitation method: solid formed in situ by change of solvent, change of pH or double decomposition (white lotion).
8. Label 'Shake well before use'; sedimentation volume F = Vu/Vo, near 1 is good.
questions.question: Define suspension. Differentiate flocculated and deflocculated suspensions. Describe the formulation excipients and general methods of preparation of suspensions.

questions.answer:
1. Emulsion: biphasic liquid in which one liquid is dispersed as globules in another immiscible liquid, stabilised by an emulsifying agent; types O/W, W/O, multiple (W/O/W, O/W/O), microemulsions.
2. Natural emulsifiers: carbohydrates (acacia, tragacanth, pectin – O/W); proteins (gelatin, egg yolk); sterol-containing (wool fat, wool alcohols, cholesterol – W/O).
3. Finely divided solids: bentonite, aluminium and magnesium hydroxide.
4. Synthetic surfactants: anionic (sodium lauryl sulphate, soaps), cationic (cetrimide), non-ionic (polysorbates O/W, sorbitan esters W/O); HLB 3–6 W/O, 8–18 O/W.
5. Identification: dilution test (O/W mixes with water); dye test (amaranth colours the continuous phase of O/W, Sudan III colours globules of O/W); conductivity (O/W conducts, bulb glows); fluorescence (O/W spotty, W/O whole field); CoCl2 paper (O/W turns blue paper pink).
6. Dry gum (continental) method: triturate oil with powdered acacia in a dry mortar; add all the water of the primary emulsion at once; triturate briskly until a clicking, creamy primary emulsion forms; dilute with remaining vehicle.
7. Ratios oil : water : gum: fixed oil 4:2:1, mineral oil 3:2:1, volatile oil 2:2:1.
8. Other methods: wet gum (mucilage first, oil added slowly), bottle (Forbes) method for volatile oils, mechanical homogenisers; label 'Shake well before use'.
questions.question: Define emulsion. Classify emulsifying agents. Describe the tests used to identify the type of emulsion and the dry gum method of preparation.

questions.answer:
1. Aromatic waters: clear saturated aqueous solutions of volatile oils or volatile substances; used as flavoured vehicles.
2. Methods: distillation; solution method (shake oil with water, with talc as distributing agent, filter); dilution of concentrated water (1 part + 39 parts water). Problem: loss and oxidation of volatile oil – store airtight, light-resistant.
3. Syrups: concentrated aqueous sucrose solutions; Simple Syrup IP 66.7% w/w; self-preserving by high osmotic pressure; flavoured or medicated.
4. Methods: solution with heat, agitation without heat, percolation, addition of medicated liquid to syrup.
5. Problems: crystallisation (cap-locking), fermentation if dilute, inversion and caramelisation with heat; preservatives for diluted syrups.
6. Elixirs: clear, sweetened hydroalcoholic solutions for oral use; non-medicated (vehicles) or medicated.
7. Method: dissolve alcohol-soluble ingredients in alcohol and water-soluble ones in water; add aqueous to alcoholic part slowly with stirring; make up and filter with talc.
8. Limitations: alcohol unsuitable for children and some patients; poor masking of salty tastes.
questions.question: Define and give the methods of preparation of aromatic waters, syrups and elixirs. Mention their problems or limitations.

questions.answer:
1. Liniments: liquid or semi-liquid preparations applied to skin with friction (rubbing).
2. Lotions: liquid preparations applied without friction, dabbed with cotton or gauze.
3. Liniments use alcoholic or oily vehicles and act as counter-irritants or rubefacients; not for broken skin. Lotions are cooling, soothing, protective or antiseptic; may be solutions or suspensions.
4. Examples: turpentine liniment, methyl salicylate liniment; calamine lotion, salicylic acid lotion. Both labelled 'For external use only'.
questions.question: Differentiate liniments and lotions with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Gargles: aqueous solutions used to treat or rinse the throat; held in the throat and spat out, not swallowed.
2. Usually supplied concentrated and diluted with warm water before use; e.g. povidone-iodine gargle, phenol gargle.
3. Mouthwashes: aqueous solutions for cleansing, deodorant and antiseptic action on mouth and gums.
4. Examples: compound sodium chloride mouthwash, chlorhexidine mouthwash; label with dilution directions and 'not to be swallowed'.
questions.question: Write notes on gargles and mouthwashes.

questions.answer:
1. Sterile (prepared aseptically or sterilised); free from particles.
2. Isotonic with tears and buffered to a comfortable, stable pH.
3. Multidose containers contain a preservative (benzalkonium chloride, chlorbutol); discard a set period after opening (usually four weeks).
4. Packed in sterile dropper containers; examples: sodium chloride eye drops, chloramphenicol eye drops.
questions.question: Give the requirements of eye drops.

questions.answer:
1. Enemas are liquid preparations given rectally.
2. Evacuant enemas empty the bowel: soap enema, oil enema, phosphate enema.
3. Retention enemas are held in the rectum for medicated, nutritive or sedative effect, e.g. arachis oil retention enema.
4. Warm to body temperature before use; packed in single-use disposable containers with a nozzle.
questions.question: What are enemas? Classify them with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Tinctures: alcoholic or hydroalcoholic solutions from vegetable drugs or chemicals (compound benzoin tincture, orange tincture).
2. Maceration: coarsely powdered drug soaked in menstruum in a closed vessel with frequent shaking (classically 7 days); strain, press the marc, mix and filter; for unorganised drugs.
3. Percolation: moistened drug packed in a percolator; menstruum flows slowly through and exhausts the drug; for organised and potent drugs.
4. Percolation extracts completely by fresh solvent; maceration is simpler but may leave drug unextracted.
questions.question: Explain maceration and percolation used for tinctures.

questions.answer: 66.7% w/w sucrose.
questions.question: What is the concentration of sucrose in Simple Syrup IP?

questions.answer: Oil reaching the lungs can cause lipid pneumonia, and oily drops impair ciliary movement.
questions.question: Why are oily nasal drops avoided?

questions.answer:
1. Ointment: soft semisolid for external application to skin or mucous membranes, with drug dissolved or dispersed in a base.
2. Ideal base: inert, non-irritant, non-sensitising, stable, compatible, easy to apply and remove, releases drug, smooth, odourless, does not support microbial growth.
3. Oleaginous (hydrocarbon): soft, hard and liquid paraffin, plastibase – greasy, occlusive, not washable.
4. Absorption bases: anhydrous (wool fat, wool alcohols, beeswax, hydrophilic petrolatum) and W/O emulsions (hydrous wool fat, cold cream) – take up water.
5. Water-removable: emulsifying ointment, cetrimide and cetomacrogol emulsifying ointments – form O/W, washable. Water-soluble: polyethylene glycols (macrogols).
6. Trituration (incorporation): finely powdered drug levigated on a slab with a little base or liquid paraffin, then rest of base added by geometric dilution.
7. Fusion: melt ingredients on a water bath in decreasing order of melting point, add drug, stir until cold; volatile ingredients added at low temperature.
8. Chemical reaction (non-staining iodine ointment) and emulsification (creams); pack in collapsible tubes or jars, label 'For external use only'.
questions.question: Define ointment. Give the ideal properties and classification of ointment bases with examples. Describe the general methods of preparation of ointments.

questions.answer:
1. Suppositories: solid dosage forms of various shapes inserted into a body orifice (rectum) where they melt, soften or dissolve; pessaries (vaginal), bougies (urethral).
2. Ideal base: melts at body temperature or dissolves in body fluids; solid at room temperature; non-toxic, non-irritant; compatible and releases drug; contracts on cooling; stable, no polymorphism problems; narrow melting–setting range; enough viscosity to keep powders suspended.
3. Fatty bases: theobroma oil (melts about 30–35 °C, polymorphic – melt gently), synthetic hard fats (hydrogenated oils).
4. Water-soluble/miscible: glycero-gelatin (hygroscopic, laxative, needs preservative, mould lubricated with liquid paraffin); polyethylene glycols (dissolve, heat-stable).
5. Emulsifying bases: fats with emulsifiers.
6. Fusion method: calibrate mould; calculate base with displacement value; melt base gently on a water bath.
7. Disperse finely powdered drug in part of the melted base, add rest, stir; pour into lubricated mould near setting point, slightly overfilling; cool, trim, remove.
8. Wrap in foil, store cool, label 'For rectal use only'; other methods: hand rolling, cold compression.
questions.question: Define suppositories. Give the properties of an ideal suppository base, types of bases and the fusion method of preparation.

questions.answer:
1. Displacement value: the number of parts by weight of drug that displace 1 part by weight of base (usually theobroma oil).
2. Need: drug and base have different densities, so the weight of base replaced is not equal to the weight of drug; ignoring this gives wrong dose and size.
3. Formula: base needed = N × E − (total drug/DV), N = number of suppositories, E = mould capacity with base.
4. Calculation: N × E = 10 × 1.0 = 10.0 g; drug = 10 × 0.2 = 2.0 g; base displaced = 2.0/1.5 = 1.33 g.
5. Base needed = 10.0 − 1.33 = 8.67 g; in practice calculate for a few extra suppositories to allow loss.
6. Finding DV: make blank and medicated batches; DV = weight of drug in medicated batch ÷ (weight of blank batch − weight of base in medicated batch).
7. Example: 6 blanks 6.0 g; 6 medicated with 40% drug weigh 7.2 g → drug 2.88 g, base 4.32 g, displaced 1.68 g, DV = 1.71.
8. For glycero-gelatin in a theobroma-oil-calibrated mould, multiply base weight by about 1.2.
questions.question: Define displacement value. How is it used in suppository preparation? Calculate the base needed for 10 suppositories each containing 200 mg of a drug (DV 1.5) in a 1 g mould.

questions.answer:
1. Ointment: soft greasy (or non-greasy) semisolid of drug in a base; e.g. sulphur ointment.
2. Cream: semisolid emulsion, O/W (vanishing, washable) or W/O (cold cream, emollient).
3. Paste: stiff semisolid with a large proportion of fine powder; less greasy, protective, absorbs exudate; e.g. compound zinc paste.
4. Gel: liquid held in a three-dimensional polymer network; clear, non-greasy; e.g. carbomer gel.
questions.question: Differentiate ointments, creams, pastes and gels.

questions.answer:
1. Advantages: useful when patient is vomiting, unconscious or cannot swallow; for children.
2. Drugs irritant to or destroyed in the stomach can be given; partly avoid first-pass metabolism; local action in rectum or vagina.
3. Disadvantages: patient dislike; slow and irregular absorption; local irritation; leakage.
4. May melt in hot weather, so need cool storage.
questions.question: Give the advantages and disadvantages of suppositories.

questions.answer:
1. Creams: heat oil phase (oils, waxes, emulsifier) and aqueous phase (water, water-soluble ingredients, preservative) separately to about 70–75 °C.
2. Add internal phase to external phase with continuous stirring; stir until the cream sets on cooling; add perfume and volatile drugs below about 40 °C.
3. Gels: sprinkle gelling agent on vehicle with stirring, let it hydrate; add drug, preservative and humectant.
4. For carbomer, add triethanolamine to neutralise and thicken; remove air bubbles; fill into tubes.
questions.question: Describe the preparation of creams and gels.

questions.answer:
1. Theobroma oil: fatty base; melts at about 30–35 °C; glycero-gelatin: water-miscible; dissolves in body fluids.
2. Theobroma oil shows polymorphism and must be melted gently; may go rancid. Glycero-gelatin is hygroscopic, may irritate and has a laxative effect; needs a preservative.
3. Theobroma oil contracts on cooling and seldom needs a lubricant (soap spirit if needed); glycero-gelatin needs an oily lubricant such as liquid paraffin.
4. Glycero-gelatin suits vaginal pessaries; it is denser, so about 1.2 × the theobroma-oil weight is used.
questions.question: Compare theobroma oil and glycero-gelatin as suppository bases.

questions.answer:
1. Bases: carry the drug (soft paraffin, wool fat, emulsifying ointment, PEG).
2. Emulsifiers and gelling agents: emulsifying wax, polysorbates; carbomer, HPMC, sodium CMC.
3. Humectants (glycerin, propylene glycol), preservatives (parabens, chlorocresol), antioxidants (BHA, tocopherol).
4. Penetration enhancers (propylene glycol, surfactants), neutralisers (triethanolamine), buffers and perfumes.
questions.question: List the excipients used in semisolid dosage forms with their functions.

questions.answer: The number of parts by weight of a drug that displaces one part by weight of the suppository base.
questions.question: Define displacement value.

questions.answer: A suppository meant for insertion into the vagina.

units.markdown:
# Unit 1: Introduction to the profession of pharmacy

This unit is the "who we are" part of the subject. It explains how pharmacy grew in India as an education, an industry and a set of organisations; what pharmacists do in shops, hospitals and factories; which official books set the standards for medicines; and how a prescription is read and handled. Expect at least one question on prescription and one on pharmacopoeias in most papers.

## 1.1 History of the profession of pharmacy in India

### Before modern pharmacy

- India has an old written tradition of medicine. **Ayurveda** texts such as the **Charaka Samhita** and **Sushruta Samhita** describe how plant, animal and mineral drugs were collected, purified and combined. **Unani** came with Persian and Arab physicians (hakims) and **Siddha** grew in South India.
- In all these systems the healer (vaidya or hakim) also prepared the medicine. Pharmacy was not yet a separate job.
- In the British period, Western (allopathic) medicines were imported and sold through a few chemist shops in port cities. Hospitals used **compounders** who learnt by assisting doctors. There was no qualification, no registration and no law on drug quality, so adulterated and spurious drugs were common.

### Milestones in pharmacy education

| Period | Milestone | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Early 20th century | Compounder training in hospitals | Informal, learnt on the job |
| 1930s | **Prof. M. L. Schroff** starts university pharmacy teaching at **Banaras Hindu University**; BHU begins a degree course in pharmacy (1937) | Schroff is remembered as the **father of pharmacy education in India** |
| 1948 | **Pharmacy Act, 1948** | Created the Pharmacy Council of India and the system of registered pharmacists |
| 1949 | **Pharmacy Council of India (PCI)** constituted | Lays down minimum standards for D.Pharm, B.Pharm, Pharm.D; approves institutions; State Pharmacy Councils keep registers |
| Later decades | Growth of D.Pharm, B.Pharm, M.Pharm and Ph.D. programmes | Shift from compounding to science-based training |
| 2008 | **Pharm.D** introduced | Six-year clinically oriented degree |
| 2014 | Credit-based PCI B.Pharm syllabus | Semester system with internal assessment |
| 2015 | **Pharmacy Practice Regulations** | Defined duties and conduct of registered pharmacists in practice |
| 2026 | B.Pharm syllabus as per **NEP 2020** (this course) | Multidisciplinary, credit-based curriculum from 2026-27 |

### Milestones in the pharmaceutical industry

- **Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works**, Calcutta, founded by **Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray** (registered as a company in 1901) is usually called the first Indian pharmaceutical company. Other early firms followed in Baroda, Bombay and elsewhere.
- **Drugs Enquiry Committee (Chopra Committee), 1930–31**, chaired by **Col. R. N. Chopra**, reported on poor-quality drugs and recommended a central drug law, a drug-testing laboratory and an Indian pharmacopoeia.
- This led to the **Drugs Act, 1940** (now the **Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940**) and the **Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945**, which control import, manufacture, sale and distribution.
- After independence, public sector units (for example Hindustan Antibiotics Ltd and Indian Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Ltd) were set up for antibiotics and bulk drugs.
- The **Patents Act, 1970** recognised only process patents for medicines, so Indian firms could make generic versions of new drugs by new routes. India became a major producer of bulk drugs and generics and is often called the **"pharmacy of the world"**.
- From 2005 product patents returned (to meet the WTO TRIPS agreement), pushing Indian firms towards research, contract manufacturing and export to regulated markets.

### Organisations connected with pharmacy

| Organisation | Main role |
| --- | --- |
| Pharmacy Council of India (PCI) | Education standards and registration under the Pharmacy Act, 1948 |
| State Pharmacy Councils | Register pharmacists in each state |
| Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), headed by the **Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI)** | Approval of new drugs and clinical trials, import control, coordination with state drug controllers |
| Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC), Ghaziabad | Publishes the IP and the National Formulary of India; runs the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India |
| Indian Pharmaceutical Association (IPA) | Professional body of pharmacists |
| Association of Pharmaceutical Teachers of India (APTI) | Body of pharmacy teachers |
| Indian Pharmaceutical Congress Association | Organises the yearly Indian Pharmaceutical Congress |
| Indian Drug Manufacturers' Association (IDMA) | Industry body of Indian drug makers |

## 1.2 Scope of the pharmacy profession

A pharmacist is the expert on medicines: how they are made, checked, stored, supplied and used. The main fields are below.

### Community (retail) pharmacy

- Receive, check and dispense prescriptions; only a **registered pharmacist** may dispense.
- Counsel patients on how and when to take medicines, storage, side effects and interactions.
- Supply over-the-counter medicines responsibly and refer patients to a doctor when needed.
- Keep records and registers required by law; store medicines properly (cold chain for vaccines and insulin).
- Health promotion: screening (blood pressure, blood sugar), advice on smoking, diet and hygiene.

### Hospital pharmacy

- Purchase, store and distribute medicines to wards and outpatients; inventory control.
- Prepare sterile and non-sterile products in the hospital (for example dilutions, IV admixtures).
- Serve on the **Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committee**, which prepares the hospital formulary.
- Drug information service for doctors and nurses.

### Clinical pharmacy

- Work with doctors on ward rounds; review prescriptions for dose, interactions and duplication.
- Monitor drug therapy and report adverse drug reactions (pharmacovigilance).
- Patient counselling at discharge, therapeutic drug monitoring, medication history.

### Industrial pharmacy, including research and development

| Department | Pharmacist's role |
| --- | --- |
| Research and development (R&D) | Pre-formulation, formulation development, stability studies, scale-up |
| Production | Manufacture of tablets, capsules, liquids, injections under Good Manufacturing Practice |
| Quality control (QC) | Testing raw materials, in-process and finished products against IP or other standards |
| Quality assurance (QA) | Documentation, validation, audits, GMP compliance |
| Regulatory affairs | Preparing dossiers and licences for approval in India and abroad |
| Marketing and sales | Product management, medical representatives |

### Other fields

Government service (Drug Inspector, Government Analyst), teaching and research, clinical research and pharmacovigilance, entrepreneurship (own pharmacy or unit), cosmetics and nutraceuticals.

## 1.3 Pharmacopoeias

**Pharmacopoeia** (Greek *pharmakon* = drug, *poiein* = to make): an official book, published under the authority of a government or recognised body, giving **standards of identity, purity and strength** of drugs and their preparations, together with test methods. A **monograph** is the entry for one substance or one preparation.

### Major pharmacopoeias

| Book | Publisher and facts | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP)** | First edition **1955**; later editions 1966, 1985, 1996, 2007, 2010, 2014, 2018 and 2022. Published by the **Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad**, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare | Official book of standards in India under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act |
| **British Pharmacopoeia (BP)** | First published **1864**; now by the British Pharmacopoeia Commission, revised every year | Official in the UK; includes European Pharmacopoeia texts |
| **United States Pharmacopeia (USP)** | First published **1820**; by the United States Pharmacopeial Convention; issued together with the National Formulary as **USP–NF** | Official in the USA; NF covers excipients |
| **British Pharmaceutical Codex (BPC)** | First published **1907** by the Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain | Gave formulae of preparations and information on drugs, dressings; later continued as the Pharmaceutical Codex |
| **International Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Int.)** | Published by the **World Health Organization** | Model standards, especially for essential medicines; a country may adopt it |
| Other pharmacopoeias | European Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Eur.), Japanese Pharmacopoeia (JP), Chinese Pharmacopoeia, Martindale (a reference book, not a pharmacopoeia) | Used for export and reference |

### National Formulary of India (NFI)

- A **formulary** is a book of formulae and information on medicines for prescribers and pharmacists.
- The NFI (first edition 1960) is now published by the **Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission**.
- It gives drug information in therapeutic groups: indications, contraindications, cautions, side effects, interactions and preparations available, helping **rational use of medicines**. Unlike the IP, it is a guide to use, not a book of legal quality standards.

### Structure and content of the Indian Pharmacopoeia

Recent editions come in several volumes. The broad layout is:

```text
Indian Pharmacopoeia
 ├── Front matter: preface, IPC members, introduction, list of changes (additions, omissions)
 ├── General Notices: rules for reading the book (meaning of "about", temperatures, storage terms,
 │                    solubility terms, "per cent" w/w, w/v, v/v, official titles)
 ├── General Chapters (Appendices): test methods (pH, melting point, UV, IR, HPLC, dissolution,
 │                    sterility, microbial limits), reagents, volumetric solutions, buffers
 ├── General Monographs: dosage forms (tablets, capsules, injections, oral liquids) – common tests
 └── Monographs: drug substances, excipients, dosage forms, vaccines and immunosera,
                 blood products, herbal products, biotechnology products, veterinary products
```

### Study of one model IP monograph (layout)

Every monograph follows a fixed order. Use paracetamol as the illustration of the layout.

| Heading | What it gives (paracetamol as illustration) |
| --- | --- |
| Title | Official name, for example **Paracetamol** (synonym: acetaminophen) |
| Formula and molecular weight | C8H9NO2, about 151.2 |
| Definition and content limit | Chemical name and the permitted range of pure drug, stated as a percentage calculated on the dried basis |
| Category | Analgesic and antipyretic |
| Dose | Usual dose range (pharmacist's reference only) |
| Description | White crystalline powder; odourless |
| Solubility | Uses standard terms (for example "sparingly soluble in water, freely soluble in ethanol") |
| Identification | Tests that prove identity: infrared spectrum compared with a reference, melting point, colour reactions |
| Tests | Purity tests: limit of related impurities (such as 4-aminophenol), heavy metals, sulphated ash, loss on drying |
| Assay | The quantitative method to find the content |
| Storage | For example, store protected from light in a well-closed container |
| Labelling | Any special statement required on the label |

**Pharmacopoeial solubility terms** (parts of solvent for 1 part of solute):

| Term | Parts of solvent |
| --- | --- |
| Very soluble | less than 1 |
| Freely soluble | 1 to 10 |
| Soluble | 10 to 30 |
| Sparingly soluble | 30 to 100 |
| Slightly soluble | 100 to 1000 |
| Very slightly soluble | 1000 to 10 000 |
| Practically insoluble | more than 10 000 |

## 1.4 Introduction to prescription

### Definition

A **prescription** is a written (or electronic) order from a registered medical practitioner (or dentist or veterinarian) to a pharmacist to prepare and/or dispense a specified medicine for a named patient, with directions for use. It is a legal document.

### Parts of a prescription

```text
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Dr. A. B. Name, MBBS, MD          Reg. No. 12345     │  1 Prescriber details
 │ Clinic address, phone                                │
 │                                   Date: 05-07-2026   │  2 Date
 │ Patient: R. Kumar   Age: 34 y   Sex: M   Wt: 62 kg   │  3 Patient details
 │ Address: ...                                         │
 │ Rx                                                   │  4 Superscription
 │   Tab. ......... 500 mg            No. 10            │  5 Inscription
 │   Make 10 such tablets / Mitte 10                    │  6 Subscription
 │   Sig. 1 tab t.d.s. p.c. for 3 days                  │  7 Signatura
 │   Refill: nil                                        │  8 Renewal
 │                               Signature of prescriber │  9 Signature
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Part | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Date | Shows when the prescription was written; helps check validity and refills |
| Name, age, sex and address of patient | Identifies the patient; age and weight are essential for children's doses |
| **Superscription** | The symbol **Rx**, from Latin *recipe* = "take thou" |
| **Inscription** | The main part: names and quantities of the ingredients (base, adjuvant, vehicle in a compounded prescription) |
| **Subscription** | Directions to the pharmacist: dosage form to make and quantity to supply |
| **Signatura** (Sig.) | Directions to the patient, to be copied on the label: dose, frequency, route, timing |
| Renewal instructions | Whether and how many times it may be refilled |
| Signature, address and registration number of prescriber | Makes the order legal and genuine |

### Types of prescriptions

- **Precompounded (ready-made)**: proprietary products such as tablets and syrups, dispensed as supplied.
- **Extemporaneous**: the pharmacist must compound the preparation (for example a mixture, ointment or powders).

### Handling of a prescription

1. **Receiving**: receive it personally and courteously; do not discuss the diagnosis loudly.
2. **Reading and checking**: check that it is legal and complete (prescriber's signature, registration number, date, patient details); check legibility, doses, frequency, duration, incompatibilities and interactions. Any doubt is cleared with the **prescriber**, not with the patient.
3. **Collecting materials**: take out the correct drugs and containers; check each label three times (when taking out, when using, when putting back).
4. **Compounding or counting**: weigh and measure accurately; prepare one prescription at a time on a clean bench.
5. **Packing**: choose a suitable container (amber bottle for light-sensitive liquids, wide-mouth jar for ointments, fluted bottle for external use where practised).
6. **Labelling**: patient name, name and strength of medicine, directions, date, pharmacy name and address, and auxiliary labels ("For external use only", "Shake well before use").
7. **Recording**: enter in the prescription register; stamp and return or retain the prescription as the law requires.
8. **Delivering and counselling**: hand over to the patient, explain dose, timing, storage, likely side effects and what to avoid.

### Common errors in prescriptions

- Illegible handwriting; look-alike or sound-alike names.
- Decimal errors: ".5 mg" read as "5 mg", "5.0 mg" read as "50 mg". Write "0.5 mg" and never put a trailing zero.
- Wrong or missing dose, frequency, route or duration; missing age or weight for children.
- Ambiguous abbreviations; incompatibility or interaction between prescribed drugs.
- Missing date, signature or registration number.

### Latin terms used in prescriptions

| Abbreviation | Latin | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rx | recipe | take thou |
| a.c. | ante cibum | before meals |
| p.c. | post cibum | after meals |
| o.d. | omni die | once a day |
| b.d. / b.i.d. | bis in die | twice a day |
| t.d.s. / t.i.d. | ter die sumendum / ter in die | three times a day |
| q.i.d. / q.d.s. | quater in die | four times a day |
| o.m. | omni mane | every morning |
| o.n. | omni nocte | every night |
| h.s. | hora somni | at bedtime |
| stat. | statim | immediately |
| s.o.s. | si opus sit | if necessary (once) |
| p.r.n. | pro re nata | when required |
| q.s. | quantum sufficit | sufficient quantity |
| ad | ad | up to |
| aq. | aqua | water |
| aq. dest. | aqua destillata | distilled water |
| M. | misce | mix |
| ft. | fiat | let it be made |
| Sig. | signa | label / write |
| div. in p. aeq. | divide in partes aequales | divide into equal parts |
| gtt. | guttae | drops |
| mist. | mistura | mixture |
| ung. | unguentum | ointment |
| p.o. | per os | by mouth |
| ss | semis | one half |
| e.m.p. | ex modo prescripto | in the manner prescribed |
| ad lib. | ad libitum | as much as desired |

## Remember

- Chopra Committee (1930–31) → Drugs Act 1940; Pharmacy Act 1948 → PCI 1949; first IP 1955.
- Prof. M. L. Schroff, BHU: father of pharmacy education in India; P. C. Ray: Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works.
- IP is published by the IPC, Ghaziabad; BP from 1864; USP from 1820; BPC from 1907; Ph. Int. by WHO; NFI is a guide to rational use, not a legal standard.
- Monograph order: title, formula, definition, category, description, solubility, identification, tests, assay, storage, labelling.
- Prescription parts: superscription (Rx), inscription (drugs), subscription (to pharmacist), signatura (to patient).
- Clear every doubt with the prescriber; check labels three times; write 0.5 mg, never .5 mg.

# Unit 2: Pharmaceutical calculations, posology, dosage forms, APIs and excipients

This unit gives you the tools used every day in dispensing: weighing and measuring in metric units, working out strengths and dilutions, making alcohol and eye drops of the right strength, calculating a child's dose, and understanding what a dosage form is made of. Numericals from this unit appear in nearly every paper. All drug names and numbers in the worked examples below are made up for practice.

## 2.1 Metric system of weights and measures

The metric (SI-based) system is the official system in the IP. Units grow or shrink in steps of 10, so conversion is only moving the decimal point.

| Quantity | Base unit | Common pharmaceutical units |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mass (weight) | gram (g) | kilogram (kg) = 1000 g; milligram (mg) = 10^-3 g; microgram (µg) = 10^-6 g; nanogram (ng) = 10^-9 g |
| Volume | litre (L) | millilitre (ml) = 10^-3 L; microlitre (µl) = 10^-6 L; 1 ml ≈ 1 cm³ |
| Length | metre (m) | centimetre (cm) = 10^-2 m; millimetre (mm) = 10^-3 m; micrometre (µm) = 10^-6 m; nanometre (nm) = 10^-9 m |

**Prefixes**: kilo (10³), centi (10^-2), milli (10^-3), micro (10^-6), nano (10^-9).

Older systems (imperial and apothecaries') are no longer official, but you may meet them: 1 grain ≈ 64.8 mg, 1 pound (lb) ≈ 0.4536 kg (so 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb), 1 fluid ounce (imperial) ≈ 28.4 ml. Household measures used in labels: **1 teaspoonful = 5 ml, 1 tablespoonful = 15 ml**.

### Scientific notation

Very large or very small numbers are written as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

| Ordinary | Scientific notation |
| --- | --- |
| 0.00025 g | 2.5 × 10^-4 g (= 250 µg) |
| 1 500 000 units | 1.5 × 10^6 units |
| 0.000001 m | 1 × 10^-6 m (= 1 µm) |

Rules: when you multiply, add the powers; when you divide, subtract them. Example: (3 × 10^-3) × (2 × 10²) = 6 × 10^-1 = 0.6.

**Tips for accurate work**: always write units; put a zero before a decimal point (0.5 not .5); never add a trailing zero (5 not 5.0); check the answer is sensible.

## 2.2 Percentage and ratio strength (dilute solutions)

| Expression | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| % w/w (weight in weight) | g of solute in 100 g of product (ointments, powders) |
| % w/v (weight in volume) | g of solute in 100 ml of product (solutions of solids) |
| % v/v (volume in volume) | ml of solute in 100 ml of product (liquids in liquids, alcohol) |
| % v/w | ml of liquid in 100 g of product |
| Ratio strength | 1 in 1000 (1:1000) means 1 g in 1000 ml for a solid in a liquid, unless stated otherwise |
| ppm | parts per million; 1 ppm = 1 mg per litre (or per kg) |

When a percentage is written without a type, the IP convention is: solids in liquids w/v, liquids in liquids v/v, solids in solids w/w.

**Worked examples**

1. 2.5 g of a drug in 50 ml solution: strength = 2.5/50 × 100 = **5% w/v**.
2. 4 g of drug in 80 g of ointment: 4/80 × 100 = **5% w/w**.
3. A 1 in 2500 solution as a percentage: 100/2500 = **0.04% w/v**.
4. Drug in 250 ml of a 1 in 400 solution: 250/400 = **0.625 g**.

### Dilution of solutions

Amount of drug does not change on dilution, so

```text
C1 × V1 = C2 × V2        (C = strength, V = volume or weight)
```

- **Example 1**: How much water must be added to 200 ml of a 25% w/v solution to make it 10% w/v? V2 = 200 × 25/10 = 500 ml. Dilute to **500 ml**, i.e. add about **300 ml** water (always "make up to volume").
- **Example 2**: Volume of a 1 in 200 stock needed to make 500 ml of a 1 in 1000 solution: V1 = 500 × (1/1000) ÷ (1/200) = **100 ml** stock, made up to 500 ml.
- **Stock solutions** are concentrated solutions kept ready so that small quantities can be measured accurately by dilution.

## 2.3 Alligation

Alligation is a quick arithmetic method for mixing two strengths to get an intermediate strength.

### Alligation medial

Finds the strength of a mixture of known quantities. Strength of mixture = Σ(quantity × strength) ÷ Σ quantity.

Example: 300 g of 10% w/w ointment mixed with 200 g of 4% w/w ointment: (3000 + 800)/500 = **7.6% w/w**.

### Alligation alternate

Finds in what proportion two strengths must be mixed.

```text
 Higher strength  10 \           / (5 − 2) = 3 parts of 10%
                      \ 5 (wanted)
 Lower strength    2 /           \ (10 − 5) = 5 parts of 2%
                                  -----------
                                   total 8 parts
```

Example: make **400 g of 5% w/w** ointment from 10% w/w and 2% w/w ointments. Parts = 3 : 5 (total 8). 10% ointment = 400 × 3/8 = **150 g**; 2% ointment = 400 × 5/8 = **250 g**.

A diluent (water, base) is treated as **0%**. Example: 500 ml of 4% w/v from a 20% w/v stock: 20 → 4 parts, 0 → 16 parts, ratio 1 : 4; take **100 ml** stock and make up to 500 ml (same as C1V1).

Check every alligation answer by alligation medial.

## 2.4 Proof spirit

- **Proof spirit** is a mixture of ethanol and water that contains **57.1% v/v** (about 49.3% w/w) ethanol at 51 °F (about 10.6 °C). It is defined as **100° proof**.
- The name comes from an old test: gunpowder soaked in the spirit could still be lit ("proved") only if the spirit was at least this strong.
- Spirit stronger than proof is **over proof (OP)**; weaker is **under proof (UP)**. 100% ethanol is 175.3° proof, i.e. 75.3 OP.
- Proof strength matters for excise duty on alcohol used in medicines.

**Formulae**

```text
Degree proof          = % v/v ethanol × 1.753      (1.753 = 100 / 57.1)
Degrees OP            = degree proof − 100
Degrees UP            = 100 − degree proof
Volume of proof spirit = volume of sample × degree proof / 100
% v/v ethanol         = degree proof / 1.753
```

**Worked examples**

1. 90% v/v alcohol: 90 × 1.753 = 157.8° proof = **57.8 OP**.
2. 40% v/v alcohol: 40 × 1.753 = 70.1° proof = **29.9 UP**.
3. Proof spirit in 2 litres of 60% v/v alcohol: 60 × 1.753 = 105.18° proof; 2000 × 105.18/100 = **2103.6 ml** of proof spirit.
4. 500 ml of spirit at 60 OP (160° proof): proof spirit = 500 × 160/100 = **800 ml**; strength = 160/1.753 = **91.3% v/v**.
5. Dilute 95% v/v alcohol to 45% v/v: by alligation 95 vs 0 → 45 parts of 95% to 50 parts water; in practice take 45 volumes of 95% alcohol and **make up to 95 volumes** with water, because alcohol and water contract on mixing.

## 2.5 Isotonic solutions

- **Osmotic pressure** depends on the number of particles in solution. **Isotonic** solutions have the same osmotic pressure as body fluids (blood, tears); **hypotonic** have less (cells swell and may burst, haemolysis); **hypertonic** have more (cells shrink, crenation).
- Blood plasma and tears freeze at **−0.52 °C**. A solution that freezes at −0.52 °C is isotonic. **0.9% w/v sodium chloride** and **5% w/v dextrose** are isotonic.
- Importance: injections (especially large volume and intrathecal), eye drops, nasal drops and wound washes should be isotonic for comfort and to avoid tissue damage.

### Method 1: Freezing point depression (FPD) method

```text
W = (0.52 − a) / b
W = g of adjusting substance per 100 ml
a = FPD of the unadjusted drug solution (°C)
b = FPD of a 1% w/v solution of the adjusting substance (NaCl: 0.576 °C)
```

Check: plain NaCl, a = 0, W = 0.52/0.576 = 0.90 g per 100 ml, which is why 0.9% is isotonic.

Example: a 1% w/v solution of drug X lowers the freezing point by 0.10 °C. NaCl needed = (0.52 − 0.10)/0.576 = **0.73 g per 100 ml**.

### Method 2: Sodium chloride equivalent (E) method

**E** = weight of NaCl that has the same osmotic effect as 1 g of the drug.

Example: make 60 ml of an isotonic 2% w/v solution of drug Y (E = 0.20).
1. Drug present = 2 × 60/100 = 1.2 g.
2. Its NaCl equivalent = 1.2 × 0.20 = 0.24 g.
3. NaCl needed for 60 ml isotonic = 0.9 × 60/100 = 0.54 g.
4. NaCl to add = 0.54 − 0.24 = **0.30 g**.

### Other methods

- **White–Vincent method**: volume of water that makes a given weight of drug isotonic, V = W × E × 111.1 (ml); the rest of the volume is made up with an isotonic vehicle. Example: 0.3 g of drug Y (E 0.20) needs 0.3 × 0.20 × 111.1 = **6.7 ml** water.
- **Molar concentration method**: uses the number of particles (osmolarity); plasma is about 290 mOsm/L.

## 2.6 Geometric dilution

Used to mix a **small amount of a potent drug** evenly with a large amount of diluent (for example lactose).

1. Weigh the drug and the diluent.
2. Put the drug in the mortar; add an **equal amount** of diluent and triturate well.
3. Add diluent equal to the amount now in the mortar and mix again.
4. Keep doubling until all the diluent is added.

```text
 drug 50 mg + diluent 50 mg  →  100 mg
 + 100 mg diluent             →  200 mg
 + 200 mg diluent             →  400 mg
 ... continue doubling until the total (for example 5 g) is reached
```

A coloured inert powder (for example a trace of carmine) can be used to check uniform mixing. In the example, 50 mg in 5 g gives a **1% w/w** trituration.

## 2.7 Posology

**Posology** (Greek *posos* = how much, *logos* = study) is the branch of pharmacy that deals with doses. A **dose** is the quantity of a drug given at one time to produce the desired effect.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Therapeutic dose | Amount that gives the desired effect |
| Minimum dose | Smallest amount that gives an effect |
| Maximum dose | Largest amount that can be given safely at one time |
| Loading dose | Larger first dose to reach the needed blood level quickly |
| Maintenance dose | Dose that keeps the level steady |
| Prophylactic dose | Dose given to prevent disease |

### Factors affecting dose

Age (children and elderly need less), body weight and body surface area, sex (pregnancy and lactation need care), route of administration, time of administration (before or after food), environment (temperature, altitude), emotional factors and placebo effect, presence of disease (liver or kidney disease reduces elimination), tolerance, idiosyncrasy and allergy, cumulation, synergism and antagonism with other drugs, accumulation and genetic factors.

### Dose calculation formulas

All give a **fraction of the adult dose**. They are approximations; for most drugs official references give doses by weight (per kg) or BSA, and the pharmacist checks these.

| Basis | Rule | Formula |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Age | **Young's rule** (children 1–12 years) | Child dose = Age (years) / (Age + 12) × Adult dose |
| Age | **Dilling's rule** | Child dose = Age (years) / 20 × Adult dose |
| Age | **Cowling's rule** | Child dose = Age at next birthday / 24 × Adult dose |
| Age | **Fried's rule** (infants under 2 years) | Infant dose = Age (months) / 150 × Adult dose |
| Body weight | **Clark's rule** | Child dose = Weight (lb) / 150 × Adult dose |
| Body weight | Per kg | Dose = dose per kg × body weight (kg) |
| Body surface area | **BSA method** (most accurate) | Child dose = BSA of child (m²) / 1.73 × Adult dose |

BSA is read from a **nomogram** (height and weight) or calculated, for example by the Mosteller formula: BSA (m²) = √[height (cm) × weight (kg) / 3600]. The average adult BSA is taken as **1.73 m²**.

**Worked fractions**

- 6-year-old by Young's rule: 6/(6 + 12) = **1/3** of the adult dose. By Dilling's rule: 6/20 = **0.3**.
- Child of 44 lb (about 20 kg) by Clark's rule: 44/150 = **0.29** of the adult dose.
- Infant of 18 months by Fried's rule: 18/150 = **0.12** of the adult dose.
- Child 120 cm tall and 25 kg: BSA = √(120 × 25/3600) = 0.91 m²; fraction = 0.91/1.73 = **0.53** of the adult dose.

## 2.8 Routes of administration

| Route | Examples of dosage forms | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oral | Tablets, capsules, syrups, suspensions | Safe, convenient; slow onset; first-pass metabolism |
| Sublingual / buccal | Sublingual tablets, lozenges | Rapid absorption; avoids first-pass effect |
| Parenteral (IV, IM, SC, intradermal) | Injections, infusions | Fast and complete; needs sterility and trained staff |
| Rectal | Suppositories, enemas | For vomiting or unconscious patients; partly avoids first pass |
| Vaginal | Pessaries, creams | Local action |
| Topical (skin) | Ointments, creams, lotions, dusting powders | Local action on skin |
| Transdermal | Patches | Systemic effect through skin over long time |
| Inhalation | Aerosols, inhalers | Lungs; rapid local action |
| Ophthalmic, otic, nasal | Eye drops, ear drops, nasal drops/sprays | Local action; eye products must be sterile |

## 2.9 Classification of dosage forms

A **dosage form** is the physical form in which a drug is given (drug + excipients made into a usable, stable product).

```text
Dosage forms
 ├── Solid:     powders, granules, tablets, capsules, pills, lozenges, suppositories*
 ├── Liquid
 │    ├── Monophasic: solutions, syrups, elixirs, linctuses, aromatic waters, drops, gargles
 │    └── Biphasic:   suspensions, emulsions
 ├── Semisolid: ointments, creams, pastes, gels, jellies, suppositories*
 └── Gaseous:   aerosols, inhalations, sprays
 (*suppositories are solid at room temperature and melt or dissolve in the body)
```

They are also classified by **route** (oral, parenteral, topical, rectal, etc.) and by **use** (internal or external).

## 2.10 Active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and excipients

### API

**Active pharmaceutical ingredient (API, drug substance)**: the substance in a product that produces the pharmacological (therapeutic) effect. Ideal characteristics: pure and of known identity; stable to light, heat, moisture and air; suitable particle size and solubility for absorption; compatible with excipients; reproducible manufacture; safe and effective at the intended dose.

### Excipients

**Excipients** are substances other than the API that are added intentionally to a dosage form to help make it, protect it, help the patient take it, or control release. They should be pharmacologically inactive at the amount used.

**Ideal characteristics of an excipient**: inert (no therapeutic effect), non-toxic and non-irritant, chemically and physically compatible with the API and other excipients, stable, does not affect bioavailability adversely, acceptable taste, colour and odour, available from reliable sources at low cost, and meets pharmacopoeial standards.

**Importance**: they make manufacture possible (flow, compression, filling), protect the drug from degradation, mask taste and odour, improve appearance and identification, control release and help absorption, and ensure uniform dose.

| Class | Function | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diluents (fillers) | Bulk up small doses | Lactose, starch, microcrystalline cellulose |
| Binders | Hold particles together | Starch paste, PVP, acacia |
| Disintegrants | Break tablets apart in fluid | Starch, sodium starch glycolate |
| Lubricants, glidants | Flow and release from machine | Magnesium stearate, talc, colloidal silica |
| Solvents and vehicles | Dissolve or carry drug | Water, ethanol, glycerin |
| Preservatives | Stop microbial growth | Parabens, benzoic acid, benzalkonium chloride |
| Antioxidants | Prevent oxidation | Ascorbic acid, BHA, sodium metabisulphite |
| Sweeteners, flavours, colours | Acceptability and identification | Sucrose, sorbitol, peppermint oil, approved dyes |
| Suspending, emulsifying agents | Stabilise biphasic liquids | Tragacanth, acacia, methylcellulose |
| Buffers, tonicity agents | Control pH, isotonicity | Phosphates, citrates, sodium chloride |
| Bases | Carry drug in semisolids and suppositories | Soft paraffin, PEG, theobroma oil |

## Remember

- Metric steps of 10; 1 teaspoon = 5 ml; 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb; write 0.5 not .5.
- C1V1 = C2V2 for dilution; alligation alternate gives parts = differences across the cross; diluent = 0%.
- Proof spirit 57.1% v/v = 100° proof; degree proof = % v/v × 1.753; OP above 100, UP below.
- Isotonic: FP −0.52 °C; 0.9% NaCl; FPD of 1% NaCl 0.576 °C; W = (0.52 − a)/b; E method subtracts the drug's NaCl equivalent.
- Geometric dilution: add diluent equal to the mixture each time.
- Young's Age/(Age + 12); Clark's Weight(lb)/150; Fried's months/150; Dilling's Age/20; BSA/1.73.
- Excipient: inert, safe, compatible, stable, cheap, official.
